title: The Woman Who Made Her Husband Sift Dust

keywords: the woman who made her husband sift dust
full_text:
In the city of Cairo lived an idle, credulous fellow named Mansur who was always searching for magical shortcuts to wealth. One afternoon, his witty wife, weary of his refusal to earn an honest living, decided to cure his gullibility with a harmless comedy.

She came home from the market with a mysterious expression, leaned close to his ear, and whispered: 'O husband, I have learned an ancient secret from a foreign alchemist! The dust of the royal jewelers’ street contains countless fragments of powdered rubies and diamond dust dropped by careless gem-cutters. If you will sift the street dust through a fine horsehair sieve for three days, you will find enough precious gems to buy an emir’s palace!'

Mansur’s eyes sparkled with greed. He borrowed a large horsehair sieve, carried three enormous sacks to the jewelers’ street, swept up all the dirt, donkey droppings, and gravel, and carried it home to his courtyard.

For three days, beneath the scorching sun, Mansur sifted dust. Clouds of grey dirt filled his nose, his eyes burned, his beard was powdered with grime, and his cough shook the house, while his wife sat on the veranda enjoying cool lemonade.

At the end of three days, Mansur crawled to his wife, holding a tiny pinch of glittering sand in his palm: 'Look, wife! Is this diamond dust?'

His wife examined the sand, laughed heartily, and said: 'No, my dear husband; that is ordinary river sand from the Nile! But look around your courtyard: you have swept the whole street, cleaned our yard, and labored harder than any porter in Cairo! If you had spent those three days carrying sacks of flour at the harbor, you would have earned twenty silver dirhams of real money.'

Mansur looked at his dusty beard, saw the humor and wisdom of her lesson, threw away the sieve, and found employment with an honest builder, having learned that easy gold is nothing but dust in the wind.
moral: Do not chase impossible rumors of easy gold; common sense and honest labor are the truest riches.
